Something is overlapping when two or more things share a common part, area, or portion — while each thing still has its own separate parts as well.

Think of it like this: imagine two circles drawn on paper, and you slide one circle slightly over the other. They are now partially on top of each other. The zone where they cross is the "overlap." Neither circle has completely swallowed the other — each still has its own space — but they share a middle zone together. That shared zone is what makes them overlapping.

The essential idea is partial sharing. Not zero sharing, not complete sharing — partial.
What Overlapping Looks Like in Real Life

The word works in several different situations, and understanding each one will make it stick permanently.

1. Physical / Spatial Overlapping

When physical objects lie on top of each other — even partially — they are overlapping.

  • Roof tiles are arranged in overlapping layers, meaning each tile covers the edge of the one below it. This is intentional — it keeps rain out.
  • When you fan out a deck of cards on a table so that each card partially covers the next one, those cards are in overlapping positions.
  • Fish scales are overlapping — each scale covers a small portion of the one behind it.

The key: they are not completely stacked (one does not fully cover the other) and they are not fully separate (they do share some area). They are in between — partially covering each other.

2. Time-based / Temporal Overlapping

Two events, periods, or schedules can overlap in time — meaning they share some of the same time period.

  • If your morning meeting runs from 9 AM to 11 AM, and your training session runs from 10 AM to 12 PM, they have overlapping schedules. That hour from 10–11 AM belongs to both.
  • If one president's term ends in January and the new one begins in January, the transition period might have overlapping duties.
  • If you were studying in two schools at the same time (say, for a semester), those enrollments are overlapping.

The key is again partial sharing: they don't fully coincide, but they aren't completely separate either. Some portion of their time runs together.

3. Conceptual / Topical Overlapping

Ideas, subjects, fields of study, or categories can also overlap — meaning they share some common ground or common content.

  • Medicine and biology are overlapping fields. They are not the same subject, but they share a large amount of common knowledge. Understanding cells, organs, and diseases belongs to both.
  • The topics of "nutrition" and "fitness" are overlapping — they are different, but they share common territory (for example, what you eat affects your workout performance).
  • Psychology and philosophy have overlapping concerns — both ask questions about the mind, consciousness, and human behavior.

When two subjects overlap in this way, it means you cannot completely separate them. Part of one lives inside the other.

4. Roles and Responsibilities

In workplaces, organizations, or teams, responsibilities can overlap — meaning more than one person or department is responsible for the same task.

  • If both the marketing team and the sales team are supposed to handle customer feedback, they have overlapping responsibilities. The same duty falls on both of them.
  • A manager and a team lead might have overlapping authority over the same group of people.

This is often something organizations try to avoid (because it creates confusion), but it happens frequently.

It helps to clearly separate "overlapping" from nearby concepts:

  • Identical means two things are completely the same — there is no separate part. Overlapping things are not identical; each has its own territory outside the shared zone.
  • Adjacent / next to each other means two things are touching at their edges but not crossing over each other. Overlapping things go further — part of one actually crosses into the space of the other.
  • Completely separate means no shared area at all. Overlapping is the opposite of this.

So "overlapping" always lives in the middle ground — not fully merged, not fully apart.

When you call two things "overlapping," you are highlighting the shared zone between them and drawing attention to the fact that they are not as separate as they might appear. It signals a relationship of partial connection.

A doctor might say two symptoms are overlapping (they share characteristics). A city planner might say two districts have overlapping boundaries. A student might say two assignments have overlapping deadlines. In every case, the word signals: these two things are not fully independent — they share something.

• "The two job descriptions were overlapping, so it was unclear who was responsible for what."
  • "She had overlapping shifts at both of her part-time jobs, which made her schedule chaotic."
  • "The two theories aren't contradictory — they are overlapping, with each one explaining part of what the other explains."
  • "The roof was built with overlapping wooden planks to make it waterproof."
  • "Their overlapping interests in music and art made them fast friends."
Overlapping describes things that partially share the same space, time, or content — where each thing still has its own distinct portion, but they also have a shared zone that belongs to both.
